questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer:
I wanted a break from my busy life in Copenhagen, where I studied full time while working a student job I felt truly miserable at. I had picked a lot of easy but boring electives during my 5th semester, which drained my energy and motivation to continue studying law in the first place. Exchange was therefore a convenient out from my job, in addition to being a much needed change of scenery.

I heard a lot of good about the academics, and W&L is a small school with a low percentage of international students, so I really had to chance to get to meet and befriend some Americans.

Fall 2024 was also an election year, so I hoped there would be a lot of interesting election-themed events going on.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: The university will send you all the information you need. Getting my VISA was a breeze, thanks to Hunter.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: The Virginia Breeze Bus will drop you off on the other side of a highway with no sidewalk, so getting into town can be a bit scary. I was picked up by my mentor, but Hunter Swanson also offered to drive me to my place on the day I arrived.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: I had issues with signing up for the student-ID because I didn't have an American phone number, but I got it done in-person at the undergrad main building in a few minutes.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: Lisa Rodocker reached out to me to let me know that one of the students at the Law School was going on a work-study in Italy during the time I would be in Lexington. We very quickly arranged that I could sublease her flat, and everything went smoothly.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: I heard housing can be quite competitive, so start looking early. Your options will be very limited since you don't have a car. The Facebook Group is "W&L House Exchange"

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The course description is very bare-bones, and you'll often only get a sentence of information about the course. The descriptions also don't list course material, exam form and date.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
You send an email to the registrar, who signs you up manually.

When a spot open up, you're sent an e-mail which brings you to a page where you can choose to accept the course.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: I arranged a zoom-meeting with Dean Drumbl to get a feel for the classes I was considering, which was very helpful. She went through each class with far greater detail than the course description, and talked about what was expected of students.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got all the classes I signed up and was wait-listed for.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Don't get scared by the wait-list.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
4/5 of my professors were truly excellent in their field of study, and just full of personality and so passionate about their field. Each class was a blast.

It's a small school, so the course offering is pretty limited.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: Your workload will easily be 2-3 times as hard as UCPH.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
Some teachers will cold-call, so be prepared to have the reading done for every class. 

Some professors don't permit laptops in their class, so I would recommend that you always print out your notes and bring them to class on paper. It also projects an image of professionalism that the professors like.

Law is studied very differently in America, and relies almost entirely on reading case law. Quimbee is so, so helpful in concisely understanding the legal reasoning and outcome of a case. Use it often.

Class sizes are a lot smaller, typically around 12-20 students. There's not the same level of anonymity, and teachers will learn your name before you learn theirs.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
LAW 683 Mass Atrocities Seminar
LAW 722 Mass Media Law
LAW 733 Criminal Procedure: Investigation
LAW 770 Employment Practices 
LAW 771 National Security Law and Practice

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Employment Practices was a waste of time, and the professor was not good at making the class interesting.

National Security Law and Practice focused on how the constitution of the U.S. limits the presidents ability to invoke national security as a justification for his exercise of power. It really highlighted how the U.S. constitution is a living document, which has been tested and forced to adapt with the passage of time. Very interesting for anyone interested in American history.

Mass Atrocities is an international law class. The final is a 17 page paper on a topic of your choice, so be prepared for that when you sign up. You won't be reading a textbook, but instead articles from all kinds of legal scholars, which can be quite different from the other classes. Professor Fyfe is great though. It's a class where you're strongly expected to participate.

Mass Media Law does not have that much reading compared to other classes, but you'll have to make a moot-court presentation before your class at least once during the semester with a partner. It's a great way to meet people actually.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: The U.S dollar gained value relative to the DKK during my time there, so I declined around 10% in purchasing power from the first to my last day.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Books are criminally expensive.

Taking the bus to D.C. is quite expensive, and ends up at 90$ for a round trip. Consider renting a car for a day if you can, it's often cheaper.

I didn't spend a lot on food because I made a deal with two of my friends who were forced to buy more meal swipes than they needed, that they would swipe for me and once they ran out for the week, I'd take them out to eat at one of the many restaurants in Lexington. I will strongly recommend going to Napa Thai.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I didn't join any clubs, but the sports facilities were amazing. There is a full gym, a giant swimming pool and pretty much every sports field you could imagine, free to use most days.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Once a month the University would host some kind of party for all law students.

W&L's version of a "Friday bar" is the flag-football tournament held each Friday afternoon right outside the university building. Afterwards, people go home and shower and then go party.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Go to flag football! People are always eager to invite people to their teams, and you don't have to play if you don't want to get dirty of injure yourself.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Thanksgiving is a big thing in America, and campus shuts down the whole week anyways. You might even get to see a whole different part of the U.S.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Very easy. People are friendly, and everyone speaks English.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer:
Be open-minded and outgoing. American Law students have already completed 4 years of undergrad college, and most have had some kind of job as well before starting. People are therefore more mature compared to UCPH, but they also have so much on their mind. Ask a lot of questions, and be sure to remind them of what you really like and appreciate about the U.S. 

Join a flag-football team.

Parties start early, and end around midnight. It's very dissimilar to the binge-drinking parties you'll be used to in Denmark, and you'll do a lot of talking.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Getting used to saying "How are you" as a greeting, and greeting people as you pass by them in the hallways.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: How people came up to talk to you, and how inclusive the social atmosphere were. If something was going on, people would make sure to invite you. I felt so welcome.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Be prepared to do 2-3 times as much reading as you're used to. You will not be relaxing during your stay.

2. Be outgoing, open-minded, and join a flag football team.

3. Participate in class, get to know your professors and take office hours with them. It'll give you some much needed confidence, since getting dropped by parachute into a new legal system can be quite overwhelming.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer:
If you need help with anything, ask. I always received an answer to my mails within a few hours, if not minutes.

Lexington is a very safe small town. I never locked the door to my apartment.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Making some amazing friends.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The workload is no joke. It is incredibly rewarding, but you will be exhausted by the time you're getting home.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
